items.stem: Which term describes the growing interconnectedness of societies worldwide, so that events in one place affect people far away?
items.answer: Globalisation
items.markingKey: Globalisation: the growing interconnectedness of societies worldwide, so that events in one place affect people far away. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “political globalisation”? Give one example.
items.answer: The growth of international organisations and agreements that shape decisions beyond the nation-state. Example: climate agreements negotiated by the United Nations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the growth of international organisations and agreements that shape decisions beyond the nation-state); 1 mark for a relevant example such as climate agreements negotiated by the United Nations. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “globalisation” and “political globalisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Globalisation: the growing interconnectedness of societies worldwide, so that events in one place affect people far away (e.g. a financial crisis in one country causing job losses in many others). Political globalisation: the growth of international organisations and agreements that shape decisions beyond the nation-state (e.g. climate agreements negotiated by the United Nations).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Young people in Accra watch the same streaming series, follow the same influencers and wear the same brands as young people in dozens of other countries. Suggest how a sceptical sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: globalisation is exaggerated: most trade and investment is still regional, nation-states remain powerful, and current levels of integration are not unprecedented (Hirst and Thompson).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A clothing company based in one country designs its products there, buys cotton from a second country, sews garments in Mumbai and sells them online worldwide. Explain how a neoliberal sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: free trade, open markets and private enterprise spread wealth and development; globalisation benefits all countries that open their economies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Isla, a sociology student, is designing a project on how far young people in Nairobi feel part of a global culture. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified; the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability. Limitations: only small samples can be studied, so results are difficult to generalise; the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far young people in Nairobi feel part of a global culture but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “global division of labour”.
items.answer: The organisation of production so that different stages take place in different countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the organisation of production so that different stages take place in different countries. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “global division of labour” and “interdependence”?
items.answer: Global division of labour: the organisation of production so that different stages take place in different countries. Interdependence: the situation in which countries rely on one another for goods, services and investment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: The table shows official data on trade for three countries studied by Tomás. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 31% | 60%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 49% | 66%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 75% | 70%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Trade as % of GDP: Country A change between 1990 and 2020?
items.answer: +29 percentage points
items.markingKey: 60 − 31 = +29 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Cape Town wants to research how far young people in Singapore feel part of a global culture. Explain one strength of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how far young people in Singapore feel part of a global culture. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how far young people in Bangkok feel part of a global culture. Explain two strengths of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way. 2. Every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how far young people in Bangkok feel part of a global culture. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that globalisation is a real, powerful process creating a borderless world in which nation-states are losing power?
items.answer: Hyperglobalism
items.markingKey: Hyperglobalism: the view that globalisation is a real, powerful process creating a borderless world in which nation-states are losing power. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “global governance”, and give one example.
items.answer: The institutions and rules that regulate issues across national borders. Example: the WTO, UN and international treaties.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the institutions and rules that regulate issues across national borders); 1 mark for a relevant example such as the WTO, UN and international treaties. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “globalisation scepticism” and “hyperglobalism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: the view that globalisation is exaggerated and that nation-states and regional economies remain dominant (e.g. pointing out that most trade is within regions). Hyperglobalism: the view that globalisation is a real, powerful process creating a borderless world in which nation-states are losing power (e.g. claims that markets now matter more than governments).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: During a global financial crisis, governments around the world spend billions to rescue banks in their own countries. Suggest how a hyperglobalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Hyperglobalism: globalisation is a powerful, real and largely irreversible process: a borderless global economy and culture are emerging, and nation-states are losing power to global markets and corporations (Ohmae).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A large technology company in Bangkok pays very little tax there by recording its profits in a country with low tax rates. Explain how a sceptical sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: globalisation is exaggerated: most trade and investment is still regional, nation-states remain powerful, and current levels of integration are not unprecedented (Hirst and Thompson).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A large technology company in Kathmandu pays very little tax there by recording its profits in a country with low tax rates. Compare how sceptical and transformationalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: globalisation is exaggerated: most trade and investment is still regional, nation-states remain powerful, and current levels of integration are not unprecedented (Hirst and Thompson). Transformationalism: globalisation is real and transforming societies, but its effects are uneven and contested; nation-states adapt and share power with global institutions rather than disappearing (Held, Giddens).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying public attitudes to globalisation.
items.answer: Strengths: they may use several methods, increasing validity; they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples. Limitations: a single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying public attitudes to globalisation but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying the power of national governments over large corporations.
items.answer: Strengths: it may be the only way to study a group that hides its activities from outsiders; it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher. Limitations: the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low; it involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the power of national governments over large corporations but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that globalisation is a real, powerful process creating a borderless world in which nation-states are losing power?
items.answer: Hyperglobalism
items.markingKey: Hyperglobalism: the view that globalisation is a real, powerful process creating a borderless world in which nation-states are losing power. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “globalisation scepticism”.
items.answer: The view that globalisation is exaggerated and that nation-states and regional economies remain dominant.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the view that globalisation is exaggerated and that nation-states and regional economies remain dominant. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “borderless world” and “regionalisation”?
items.answer: Borderless world: Ohmae’s idea that national borders are becoming irrelevant to economic activity. Regionalisation: the concentration of trade and investment within regional blocs rather than truly global flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Hirst and Thompson argued that the extent of globalisation has been exaggerated. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Hirst and Thompson argued the world economy was as open before 1914, most TNCs have a clear home base, and trade is concentrated in a few regions. Criticism: Critics argue they underestimated new forms of digital and financial globalisation.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Globalisation scepticism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Zara is planning a study of public attitudes to globalisation. Explain one limitation of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of public attitudes to globalisation. [2]

items.stem: Ana is planning a study of the power of national governments over large corporations. Explain two strengths of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Once trust is gained, members of marginalised groups may be willing to talk openly. 2. Rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the power of national governments over large corporations. [4]

items.stem: Zara, a sociology student, is designing a project on the power of national governments over large corporations. Explain one strength and two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strength: a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: 1. interviewer bias may still affect answers. 2. samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the power of national governments over large corporations. [6]

items.stem: International trade data show where three regions’ exports go. Table: share of each region’s exports going to countries in the same region (%) | 2000 | 2020. Europe | 72% | 73%. Asia | 55% | 57%. North America | 49% | 46%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Europe between 2000 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that globalisation is exaggerated because most trade is regional.
items.answer: (a) 73 − 72 = +1 percentage point. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Europe, Asia; the figure fell for North America; Europe had the highest figure for 2020. Regional trade agreements and geography encourage regional trade. Qualifications: Global supply chains, digital trade and finance are not captured by export shares; some regions trade mainly with the rest of the world. The data also come from official statistics of 3 regions in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 72 and 73; 1 mark for +1 percentage point (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the shrinking of the world as communication and transport technologies reduce the time it takes to connect distant places?
items.answer: Time-space compression
items.markingKey: Time-space compression: the shrinking of the world as communication and transport technologies reduce the time it takes to connect distant places. [1]

items.stem: Which term describes the shrinking of the world as communication and transport technologies reduce the time it takes to connect distant places?
items.answer: Time-space compression
items.markingKey: Time-space compression: the shrinking of the world as communication and transport technologies reduce the time it takes to connect distant places. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “disembedding” and “digital divide”?
items.answer: Disembedding: Giddens’s term for the lifting out of social relations from local contexts. Digital divide: unequal access to digital technologies between and within countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A family in Jakarta speaks daily by video call with relatives in three other countries and sends money to them through a phone app. Suggest how a sceptical sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: globalisation is exaggerated: most trade and investment is still regional, nation-states remain powerful, and current levels of integration are not unprecedented (Hirst and Thompson).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Singapore wants to research internet access in rural and urban areas. Explain one strength and one limitation of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this study.
items.answer: Strength: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years. Limitation: being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of internet access in rural and urban areas. [4]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “global village” and “disembedding”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Global village: McLuhan’s idea that electronic media make the world feel like a single community (e.g. people across the world watching the same live event). Disembedding: Giddens’s term for the lifting out of social relations from local contexts (e.g. friendships maintained entirely online).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying how migrants use technology to keep in touch with family.
items.answer: Strengths: it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts; the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how migrants use technology to keep in touch with family but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for studying internet access in rural and urban areas.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying internet access in rural and urban areas but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the integration of national economies through trade, investment, finance and production across borders?
items.answer: Economic globalisation
items.markingKey: Economic globalisation: the integration of national economies through trade, investment, finance and production across borders. [1]

items.stem: State one example of political globalisation.
items.answer: International climate agreements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. international climate agreements. [1]

items.stem: Held argued that globalisation has economic, political, cultural and military dimensions that are transforming the world. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Held and colleagues argued globalisation is multi-dimensional and reshapes state power rather than ending it. Criticism: Hyperglobalists argue the decline of the state is more advanced.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Transformationalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows official data on trade for three countries studied by Ravi. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 22% | 42%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 41% | 56%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 79% | 88%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Trade as % of GDP: Country B change between 1990 and 2020?
items.answer: +15 percentage points
items.markingKey: 56 − 41 = +15 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows official data on trade for three countries studied by Tariq. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 31% | 47%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 49% | 74%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 64% | 78%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Trade as % of GDP: Country C between 1990 and 2020. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) 78 − 64 = +14 percentage points. (b) The figure rose for Trade as % of GDP: Country A, Trade as % of GDP: Country B, Trade as % of GDP: Country C; Trade as % of GDP: Country C had the highest figure for 2020.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 64 and 78; 1 mark for +14 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: Official statistics on trade for three countries are shown below. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 24% | 51%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 57% | 76%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 72% | 73%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Trade as % of GDP: Country B between 1990 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that economic globalisation has transformed national economies.
items.answer: (a) 76 − 57 = +19 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Trade as % of GDP: Country A, Trade as % of GDP: Country B, Trade as % of GDP: Country C; Trade as % of GDP: Country B had the highest figure for 2020. TNCs organise production across borders. Qualifications: Sceptics note trade is often regional rather than global; some economies were already very open; statistics do not show who benefits. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 57 and 76; 1 mark for +19 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.answer: Globalisation scepticism
items.markingKey: Globalisation scepticism: the view that globalisation is exaggerated and that nation-states and regional economies remain dominant. [1]

items.stem: State one argument used by sceptics to challenge claims about globalisation.
items.answer: TNCs keep a clear national home base.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. TNCs keep a clear national home base. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Ohmae meant by arguing that nation-states have become “unnatural” business units in a borderless world economy.
items.answer: Ohmae argued global consumers, TNCs and markets have made national economies and governments far less important.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Ohmae argued global consumers, TNCs and markets have made national economies and governments far less important. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the hyperglobalist and sceptic views of globalisation.
items.answer: Hyperglobalists see globalisation as real and powerful, creating a borderless world where nation-states decline (Ohmae); sceptics argue it is exaggerated, trade is regional and states remain powerful (Hirst and Thompson).

items.stem: Which term describes Castells’s term for a society organised around digital networks of information?
items.answer: Network society

items.stem: Explain Harvey’s argument that capitalism drives time-space compression to speed up production and profit, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Harvey argued time-space compression results from capitalism’s need to reduce turnover time of capital. Criticism: Others see technology and culture as independent drivers.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows internet use from international surveys of around 500 adults in each group of countries. Table: percentage of adults using the internet | 2010 | 2023. High-income countries | 72% | 92%. Middle-income countries | 30% | 74%. Low-income countries | 6% | 29%. The digital divide reflects global inequality. Qualifications: The gap in percentage points between rich and poor countries remains large; access does not mean equal quality or skills; rural and gender gaps persist within countries. The data also come from official statistics of 500 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (66 and 63); 1 mark for “narrowed”. items.answer: The situation in which countries rely on one another for goods, services and investment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the situation in which countries rely on one another for goods, services and investment. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between economic and cultural globalisation, using an example of each.
items.answer: Economic globalisation: integration of production, trade and finance (e.g. global supply chains); cultural globalisation: spread of cultural products and values (e.g. global music streaming and brands).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: Official statistics on trade for three countries are shown below. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 22% | 49%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 55% | 66%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 73% | 69%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Trade as % of GDP: Country A change between 1990 and 2020?
items.answer: +27 percentage points
items.markingKey: 49 − 22 = +27 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows official data on trade for three countries studied by Ines. Table: trade (exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP | 1990 | 2020. Trade as % of GDP: Country A | 35% | 48%. Trade as % of GDP: Country B | 59% | 70%. Trade as % of GDP: Country C | 77% | 91%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Trade as % of GDP: Country A between 1990 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) (48 − 35) ÷ 35 × 100 = 37.1%. (b) The figure rose for Trade as % of GDP: Country A, Trade as % of GDP: Country B, Trade as % of GDP: Country C; Trade as % of GDP: Country C had the highest figure for 2020.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (48 − 35) ÷ 35 × 100; 1 mark for 37.1% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research how far young people in Toronto feel part of a global culture.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability. Limitations: only small samples can be studied, so results are difficult to generalise; participants who know they are being studied may change their behaviour (the Hawthorne effect or demand characteristics). Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far young people in Toronto feel part of a global culture but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that globalisation is real and significant but uneven, reshaping rather than replacing the nation-state?
items.answer: Transformationalism
items.markingKey: Transformationalism: the view that globalisation is real and significant but uneven, reshaping rather than replacing the nation-state. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “regionalisation”?
items.answer: The concentration of trade and investment within regional blocs rather than truly global flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the concentration of trade and investment within regional blocs rather than truly global flows. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Sceptics argue nation-states have lost most of their power.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Sceptics argue states remain powerful; it is hyperglobalists who claim states are declining.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain the transformationalist view of globalisation.
items.answer: Globalisation is real and significant, but uneven and open-ended; it reshapes rather than ends state power, creating global governance; local cultures adapt global influences (Held, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each developed point up to 3. [3]

items.stem: The table shows the destination of exports for three regions, from international trade statistics. Table: share of each region’s exports going to countries in the same region (%) | 2000 | 2020. Europe | 69% | 66%. Asia | 50% | 54%. North America | 52% | 50%. By how many percentage points did the figure for North America change between 2000 and 2020?
items.answer: -2 percentage points
items.markingKey: 50 − 52 = -2 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Grace is planning a study of the power of national governments over large corporations. Explain one limitation of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: A single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the power of national governments over large corporations. [2]

items.stem: A large technology company in Karachi pays very little tax there by recording its profits in a country with low tax rates. Explain how a transformationalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Transformationalism: globalisation is real and transforming societies, but its effects are uneven and contested; nation-states adapt and share power with global institutions rather than disappearing (Held, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying the power of national governments over large corporations.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: hard-to-reach or deviant groups are unlikely to be on a sampling frame or to return a questionnaire; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the power of national governments over large corporations but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: International trade data show where three regions’ exports go. Table: share of each region’s exports going to countries in the same region (%) | 2000 | 2020. Europe | 72% | 74%. Asia | 55% | 56%. North America | 45% | 41%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Europe between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that globalisation is exaggerated because most trade is regional.
items.answer: (a) (74 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100 = 2.8%. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Europe, Asia; the figure fell for North America; Europe had the highest figure for 2020. Sceptics point to regionalisation: much trade stays within regional blocs. Qualifications: Global supply chains, digital trade and finance are not captured by export shares; some regions trade mainly with the rest of the world. The data also come from official statistics of 3 regions in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (74 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100; 1 mark for 2.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes unequal access to digital technologies between and within countries?
items.answer: Digital divide
items.markingKey: Digital divide: unequal access to digital technologies between and within countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which communication technology has contributed to globalisation.
items.answer: Instant communication allows global business and finance; social media spreads culture and ideas; diasporas stay connected; global social movements organise online; news travels instantly.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: In a rural region near Manila, only one household in five has internet access, while in the city centre almost every home is connected. Suggest how a transformationalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Transformationalism: globalisation is real and transforming societies, but its effects are uneven and contested; nation-states adapt and share power with global institutions rather than disappearing (Held, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating internet access in rural and urban areas. Explain two strengths of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: 1. They are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years. 2. They show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to internet access in rural and urban areas. [4]

items.stem: International data (based on surveys of about 200 adults per country group) show internet use. Table: percentage of adults using the internet | 2010 | 2023. High-income countries | 68% | 84%. Middle-income countries | 20% | 61%. Low-income countries | 7% | 24%. (a) Calculate the gap between Middle-income countries and High-income countries in 2010 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the digital divide is closing.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 48 percentage points; 2023: 23 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for High-income countries, Middle-income countries, Low-income countries; High-income countries had the highest figure for 2023. Infrastructure investment is lower in poorer countries. Qualifications: The gap in percentage points between rich and poor countries remains large; access does not mean equal quality or skills; rural and gender gaps persist within countries. The data also come from official statistics of 200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (48 and 23); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]
